title: Ayushman Bharat covers seniors above 70. Are governmental schemes alone enough to secure their care?
summary: Hemanshu Jain, Founder & CEO, Khyaal, explains why financial health cover must be supported by technology, private insurance and coordinated care to meet the needs of India's ageing population
thbAction: Map the news to THB's provider CRM for referral growth, patient lifecycle engagement, and multi-facility relationship management across hospital and provider networks.
contentHtml:
When the government extended Ayushman Bharat’s INR 5 lakh annual health cover to every citizen above 70, irrespective of income, six crore senior citizens across 4.5 crore families became eligible for the scheme. For a country where growing old has historically meant financial dependence on children or pensions, it marked an important step towards making healthcare more financially accessible for India’s ageing population and recognised the growing need for senior-focused healthcare support.

However, financial coverage is only one part of the healthcare journey. For many seniors, accessing the full benefits of such schemes depends on a broader support ecosystem—one that helps them understand their entitlements, navigate hospital networks, complete documentation, book appointments, arrange transport, and receive timely follow-up care. As India’s elderly population continues to grow, the conversation must evolve from expanding healthcare coverage to strengthening the systems that enable seniors to effectively access and utilise it. The real opportunity lies in complementing government initiatives with technology, community support, and age-friendly services that bridge the gap between policy and practice.

Building a continuum of care

As India’s elderly population grows, healthcare needs to become more continuous than episodic. While hospitalisation cover provides essential financial protection during major medical events, healthy ageing also depends on a broader ecosystem of preventive, outpatient, and long-term care services.

For most senior citizens, healthcare is shaped less by one-time hospital admissions and more by regular doctor consultations, medication management, routine diagnostics, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, and the ongoing management of chronic conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or arthritis. Supporting these everyday needs helps seniors maintain their quality of life and, in many cases, reduces the likelihood of hospitalisation in the first place.

Equally important is ensuring that seniors are able to access the benefits available to them. Awareness, timely enrolment, simple documentation processes, digital assistance, and guidance in navigating healthcare systems all play a vital role in translating policy into real-world outcomes. As healthcare becomes increasingly digitised, support mechanisms that help seniors understand their insurance benefits and access services with confidence become just as important as financial coverage itself.

Digital innovation in senior healthcare

From comparing plans and completing enrollment to accessing policy documents and tracking claims, digital-first solutions are reducing paperwork and making insurance more accessible. They also allow seniors to explore supplementary covers and top-up plans that complement existing health insurance, enabling them to build more comprehensive protection based on their evolving healthcare needs.

Artificial intelligence is further enhancing this experience. AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can answer insurance-related queries in simple, conversational language, explain policy benefits and exclusions, guide users through claim procedures, and recommend suitable plans based on individual requirements. Instead of navigating lengthy policy documents or relying entirely on family members, seniors can receive personalised guidance at their own pace. 

The role of private insurance in strengthening care

This is where private insurers and senior-care providers have an important role to play as complementary partners in delivering more comprehensive healthcare.

Around the world, healthcare systems increasingly rely on layered models of protection. Singapore’s MediShield Life, for example, was deliberately built to cover catastrophic costs rather than the full spectrum of ageing-related care, which is why an estimated 70 per cent of Singaporeans still buy supplementary private insurance on top of it. Similarly, China’s approach also offers a useful precedent for why layering matters. Its long-term care insurance pilots, running in select cities since 2016, were introduced specifically because basic medical insurance, however widespread, did not address the home and community-based care that a rapidly ageing population needed. The pilots did not replace China’s public insurance architecture. They were layered on top of it to close a gap the base scheme was never designed to cover.

India is witnessing a similar evolution. Private insurers are increasingly designing products specifically for seniors, moving beyond conventional hospitalisation benefits to include OPD consultations, chronic disease management, preventive health check-ups, physiotherapy, home nursing, teleconsultations, and wellness programmes. These services complement public health coverage by supporting seniors before, during, and after major medical events.

For families whose children live in different cities or countries, these services also provide an added layer of reassurance through care coordination, health monitoring, and easier navigation of medical services. In this way, private insurance contributes not only financial protection but also continuity of care.

Towards an integrated healthcare ecosystem

As India’s population continues to age, healthcare will increasingly require collaboration across public institutions, private insurers, healthcare providers, and technology platforms. Government-backed insurance schemes create an essential foundation by expanding access to hospital care, while private insurance and age-tech innovations can enhance that foundation through preventive services, personalised care, digital support, and long-term health management.

This integrated approach benefits everyone. Seniors receive more holistic and accessible care, families gain greater confidence in managing their loved ones’ health, healthcare providers can intervene earlier through preventive care, and hospitals can focus resources on patients requiring acute treatment. Ultimately, the future of senior healthcare lies not in choosing between public and private systems, but in enabling them to work together. Together, these complementary layers can help build a healthcare ecosystem that responds not only to medical emergencies but also to the everyday realities of ageing.
